name: PRP microneedling (vampire facial)

lead: PRP microneedling, marketed as the vampire facial, combines microneedling with platelet-rich plasma prepared from the client's own blood. It is offered for skin texture, acne scars and general rejuvenation, and gained attention through celebrity endorsement in the 2010s.

Blood is spun in a centrifuge to concentrate platelets, which carry growth factors, and the plasma is applied during or after microneedling. Proponents say the growth factors boost healing and collagen production. Studies of microneedling are mostly small, and Wikipedia describes the added efficacy of PRP as in question pending scientific studies. On looksmax.org, users post before-and-after accounts and discuss DIY variants such as PRP creams.

paras: A clinic draws blood, processes it, and applies the plasma while a microneedling device makes tiny punctures in the skin. It is typically done as a series of sessions spaced weeks apart, with redness and swelling for a few days afterward.

The main concern raised in sources is infection when procedures are done in non-medical settings with poor infection control. In April 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses among patients of an unlicensed Albuquerque spa; about 200 other clients and partners tested negative. PRP is exempt from FDA regulation as a product, while the preparation devices need clearance.

angle.text: The vampire facial pairs microneedling with a person's own platelet-rich plasma to remodel collagen for smoother skin and softer acne scars. Microneedling itself is studied for scars, while the added benefit of PRP is in question pending studies.

lead: PRP microneedling, widely marketed as the vampire facial, is a cosmetic procedure that combines microneedling with platelet-rich plasma (PRP), a concentrate of a person's own blood plasma that is rich in platelets. It is offered for skin rejuvenation and acne scarring [1][2].

PRP is made by centrifuging a blood sample to remove most red cells while retaining platelets, which carry growth factors and cytokines; Wikipedia says the aim is to concentrate platelets to three to five times normal levels [1]. Platelet concentrates differ in their preparation and are classified into several types in the literature [3]. Wikipedia reports that vampire facials grew popular in the 2010s with celebrity endorsement and usually involve microneedling [1].

The evidence for PRP varies by use. A 2009 review described it as promising but not proven [1], and Wikipedia's microneedling article states that combining microneedling with PRP has efficacy in question pending scientific studies [2]. Safety attention rose in April 2024, when the CDC reported HIV cases linked to a New Mexico spa [1][2].
infobox: Skin texture, acne scars, rejuvenation; PRP also used for hair
PRP exempt from pathway; preparation devices need FDA clearance [1]

paras: Microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy, involves repeatedly puncturing the skin with small sterile needles [2]. In the vampire facial, PRP prepared from the client's blood is applied to the skin around the needling [1]. Preparation varies by person and facility [1].

PRP itself has a longer history. Wikipedia states that the term platelet-rich plasma was first used in 1954, that PRP was used in an open-heart surgery procedure in Italy in 1987, and that it was first considered for hair loss conditions in 2006 [1].

Wikipedia reports mixed evidence for PRP across medical uses. A 2014 Cochrane review found very weak evidence of short-term pain reduction in tendon conditions, while 2019 and 2024 meta-analyses reported benefits in knee osteoarthritis and ulcers; PRP is reported to help hair loss conditions, although this article does not assess those studies [1].

For microneedling, Wikipedia describes the evidence as limited and mostly small studies, with some studies of microneedling plus minoxidil reporting better hair outcomes than minoxidil alone [2]. The same article says the efficacy of microneedling with PRP is in question pending scientific studies [2]. No controlled trial of facial PRP microneedling was loaded for this article.

Wikipedia reports low adverse-effect rates for PRP in most trials, with weak evidence of harm [1]. The main risk it identifies for microneedling is infection when treatments are done in non-medical settings by untrained staff [2].

In April 2024 the CDC reported that three women diagnosed with HIV had been patients at a spa in Albuquerque, New Mexico, after receiving vampire facials; about 200 other former clients and partners tested negative. Officials found the operator was unlicensed and had reused blood-contaminated single-patient equipment [1][2].
Wikipedia notes that the FDA does not regulate PRP itself, so clinical use is off label, while the devices used to prepare PRP require clearance [1].

On looksmax.org, members post personal accounts of treatments. One poster describes PRP microneedling for acne scars left after steroid use, reporting that skin looked better the next day and that they planned further sessions, with one reply asking for a different guide [4]. Other threads discuss PRP for hair loss, with the original poster sharing a consumer health article, and homemade PRP creams or serums intended to be applied after vampire facials, with the poster citing a study whose authors, in their words, had conflicts of interest. Other thread titles show interest in at-home PRP, PRP for under-eyes and sourcing of PRP tubes. Such posts are individual accounts and not controlled evidence.
